title: Inversion 2
subtitle: Rarely do we ... / So successful was her business ...
summary: Invert subject and auxiliary after negative and only adverbials, after so and such, and after neither and nor.

lesson.heading: Negative time adverbials
lesson.text: In formal and literary language we often begin a clause with a negative adverbial. The subject and the first auxiliary then change places, and **do** appears with a simple tense.

examples.text: **Seldom do we have** goods returned to us because they are faulty.
**Hardly had everybody taken** their seats when Dr Lee began her lecture.

lesson.note: The adverbials in this group: never (before), rarely, seldom; barely / hardly / scarcely ... when / before; no sooner ... than.

lesson.heading: only + a time expression or a prepositional phrase
lesson.text: **only** at the front of a clause also brings inversion - with a time expression (only after, only later, only if, only once, only then, only when) or with other prepositional phrases (only by ..., only in ..., only with ...).

examples.text: She bought a newspaper and some milk at the shop on the corner. **Only later did she realise** that she'd been given the wrong change.
**Only when she apologises will I speak** to her again.
**Only by chance had Carl discovered** where the birds were nesting.
Maria had to work in the evenings. **Only in this way was she able** to complete the report.

lesson.note: Inversion can also follow a whole clause beginning only after / if / when or not until: Not until the train pulled into the station did Miguel find that his coat had gone.

lesson.heading: at no time, on no account, under no circumstances
lesson.text: Fixed negative phrases such as **at no time, in no way, on no account** and **under / in no circumstances** work the same way.

examples.text: **At no time did they** actually break the rules of the game.
**Under no circumstances are passengers permitted** to open the doors themselves.

lesson.heading: not only, not until, not a ..., little
lesson.text: Expressions with **not** - not only, not until, not since, not for one moment, not a + noun - and **little** with a negative meaning also require inversion.

examples.text: **Not until August did the government order** an inquiry into the accident.
**Not a word had she written** since the exam had started.
**Little do they know** how lucky they are to live in such a wonderful house.
examples.note: = they don't know, or they don't know sufficiently

lesson.heading: so + adjective ... that; such + be ... that
lesson.text: We can front **so + adjective** to emphasise the adjective, and **such + be** to emphasise the extent or degree of something. In both cases the subject and first auxiliary are inverted.

examples.text: **So successful was her business**, that Lana was able to retire at the age of 50.
**So dangerous did weather conditions become**, that all mountain roads were closed.
**Such is the popularity** of the play that the theatre is likely to be full every night.

lesson.heading: neither and nor
lesson.text: We use inversion after **neither** and **nor** when they begin a clause that adds a negative point to a previous negative one.

examples.text: For some time after the explosion Jack couldn't hear, and **neither could he see**.
The council never wanted the new supermarket to be built, **nor did local residents**.

lesson.note: The same order appears in the short replies Neither / Nor do I, Neither / Nor does Diane, So do I, So does Maya.

lesson.text: After a negative or only adverbial at the front, use question word order: the auxiliary comes before the subject, and do appears if there is no other auxiliary.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite 'The public was never in any danger': At no time ___ the public in any danger.
exercises.explanation: After At no time the verb comes before the subject.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite 'A new film has not often before produced such positive reviews': Rarely ___ a new film produced such positive reviews.
exercises.explanation: Rarely at the front brings the auxiliary in front of the subject.

exercises.prompt: Under no circumstances ___ to open the doors themselves.
exercises.explanation: Under no circumstances is a negative adverbial, so the auxiliary are goes before the subject.

exercises.statement: Hardly the evacuation had been completed when the wind changed direction.
exercises.explanation: Hardly had the evacuation been completed when the wind changed direction. After hardly the auxiliary comes before the subject.

exercises.prompt: Match the halves of these so and such sentences.

pairs.left: Such was the strength of the earthquake
pairs.right: that few buildings were left standing.

pairs.left: Such is her dominance in the sport
pairs.right: that she hasn't lost a match for over three years.
that even their parents couldn't tell them apart.
that it even took a computer three days to solve it.
that most of the students went to sleep.

pairs.left: Such is the popularity of the play
pairs.right: that the theatre is likely to be full every night.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite 'He only felt entirely relaxed with close friends and family': Only with close friends and family ___ entirely relaxed.
exercises.explanation: There is no auxiliary in the original, so do is added: did he feel.

exercises.prompt: For some time after the explosion Jack couldn't hear, and ___.
exercises.explanation: neither at the front of a clause is followed by auxiliary + subject.

exercises.statement: 'At no time did the fires pose a real threat,' said one local man.
exercises.explanation: Correct. At no time + did + subject + bare infinitive.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite 'He has only been acknowledged to be a great author in the last few years': Only in the last few years ___ been acknowledged to be a great author.
exercises.explanation: Only in + phrase puts the auxiliary has in front of the subject he.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite 'The match won't be cancelled unless the pitch is frozen' beginning Only if ... .
exercises.answer: Only if the pitch is frozen will the match be cancelled.
exercises.explanation: Inversion follows the whole only if clause, not the words inside it.

exercises.statement: So upset some elderly residents are that they are threatening to complain to their MP.
exercises.explanation: So upset are some elderly residents that they are threatening to complain to their MP. Fronted so + adjective requires inversion.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite 'I didn't know then that Carmen and I would be married one day' beginning Little ... .
exercises.answer: Little did I know then that Carmen and I would be married one day.
exercises.explanation: little has a negative meaning here, so do is added and inverted.
